source_row.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"Fairly few specific dietary modifications actually being needed for a client managing heart failure at home","B":"A single, universal diet plan applied in essentially the same way to every heart failure client seen in clinic","C":"Sodium restriction, fluid management, and overall heart-healthy eating patterns, individualized to the client's specific needs","D":"Mainly caloric intake alone, with fairly little attention paid to the other dietary components that matter for heart failure"}}
source_row.rationale: Comprehensive heart failure dietary education typically addresses sodium restriction, fluid management, and overall heart-healthy eating patterns, individualized to the client's specific condition, severity, and any additional comorbidities such as diabetes.
source_row.source_name: AHA — Heart Failure Dietary Education Guidelines
source_row.source_detail: Components of Comprehensive HF Dietary Education

source_row.stem: A nurse teaches energy conservation techniques to a client with heart failure and significant fatigue. These techniques include:
source_row.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"Prioritizing important tasks, sitting during activities when possible, and spreading tasks throughout the day rather than completing everything at once","B":"Avoiding any modification to the client's usual daily routine, since pacing is not generally considered helpful for this particular population","C":"Completing all household tasks as quickly as possible without taking any breaks at all throughout the entire day","D":"A concept generally considered to carry fairly little relevance to how heart failure symptoms are managed on a day-to-day basis"}}
source_row.rationale: Energy conservation techniques for a client with heart failure and fatigue include prioritizing important tasks, sitting during activities when possible (such as while preparing meals), and spreading tasks throughout the day rather than completing everything at once, helping manage limited energy reserves.
source_row.source_name: AHA — Energy Conservation Strategies in Heart Failure
source_row.source_detail: Practical Energy Conservation Techniques

source_row.stem: A nurse encourages a client with heart failure to maintain a daily symptom diary, tracking weight, symptoms, and activity level. This tool helps:
source_row.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"Taking the place of the ongoing provider visits the client would otherwise still need to attend on a regular, scheduled basis","B":"Carrying fairly little established value for a client trying to manage heart failure symptoms independently at home each day","C":"Applying mainly to clients who are newly diagnosed with heart failure, rather than to clients living with longer-standing disease","D":"Identify patterns and trends over time, supporting more informed conversations with the healthcare team and earlier recognition of clinical changes"}}
source_row.rationale: A heart failure symptom diary helps identify patterns and trends over time (such as gradual symptom changes), supporting more informed conversations with the healthcare team and earlier recognition of clinical changes, a valuable ongoing self-management tool throughout the disease course.
source_row.source_name: AHA — Heart Failure Self-Management Tools
source_row.source_detail: Value of Symptom Diary Tracking

source_row.stem: A nurse counsels a client about modifiable risk factors for developing heart failure. These include:
source_row.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"Mainly inherited genetic factors, with fairly little modifiable component involved in a person's overall risk","B":"Risk factors considered relevant mainly to clients already diagnosed with heart disease, rather than to the general population","C":"Fairly few modifiable risk factors having actually been established for the development of heart failure itself","D":"Hypertension, coronary artery disease, diabetes, and obesity, among other factors that can be addressed to help reduce heart failure risk"}}
source_row.rationale: Modifiable risk factors for developing heart failure include hypertension, coronary artery disease, diabetes, and obesity, among others, which can be addressed through lifestyle modification and appropriate medical management to help reduce heart failure risk.
source_row.source_name: AHA — Heart Failure Prevention and Risk Factor Guidelines
source_row.source_detail: Modifiable Risk Factors for Heart Failure

source_row.stem: A nurse ensures a client with heart failure is referred to cardiac rehabilitation upon discharge. This referral is important because cardiac rehabilitation is associated with:
source_row.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"Improved functional capacity, quality of life, and potentially reduced hospitalization and mortality when appropriately utilized","B":"Increasing the client's symptom burden overall, without providing any offsetting improvement in outcomes","C":"Carrying fairly little established benefit for clients living with heart failure specifically","D":"Benefits considered limited mainly to clients recovering from a myocardial infarction, rather than heart failure broadly"}}
source_row.rationale: Cardiac rehabilitation referral for heart failure clients is important because participation is associated with improved functional capacity, quality of life, and potentially reduced hospitalization and mortality, extending benefits recognized in cardiac rehabilitation beyond post-myocardial infarction populations alone.
source_row.source_name: AACVPR/AHA — Cardiac Rehabilitation in Heart Failure
source_row.source_detail: Benefits of Cardiac Rehabilitation in HF

source_row.stem: A nurse counsels a client with heart failure about heart-healthy lifestyle modifications. Recommendations generally include:
source_row.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"Lifestyle factors being considered relevant mainly before a heart failure diagnosis, rather than afterward during ongoing management","B":"Fairly few established lifestyle factors actually being relevant to how heart failure is managed day to day","C":"Complete avoidance of physical activity altogether as the main lifestyle recommendation for this population","D":"Regular appropriate physical activity, smoking cessation, limiting alcohol intake, and adherence to dietary recommendations"}}
source_row.rationale: Heart-healthy lifestyle recommendations for clients with heart failure generally include regular appropriate physical activity (as tolerated and guided by the care team), smoking cessation, limiting alcohol intake, and adherence to dietary recommendations, supporting ongoing disease management.
source_row.source_name: AHA — Heart-Healthy Lifestyle Recommendations for Heart Failure
source_row.source_detail: Lifestyle Modification in Heart Failure Management

source_row.stem: A nurse screens a client with chronic heart failure for anxiety and depression. This screening is important because:
source_row.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"These conditions are common in chronic heart failure and can negatively impact self-care adherence and overall quality of life, making identification important","B":"Screening generally being avoided altogether by the care team out of concern that it may cause the client unnecessary emotional distress","C":"Anxiety and depression being considered quite uncommon overall among clients who are living with chronic, long-standing heart failure","D":"Mental health screening carrying fairly little established relevance to how heart failure is actually managed in clinical practice"}}
source_row.rationale: Screening for anxiety and depression is important in chronic heart failure because these conditions are common in this population and can negatively impact self-care adherence, symptom burden, and overall quality of life, making early identification and appropriate support valuable.
source_row.source_name: AHA — Psychosocial Considerations in Heart Failure
source_row.source_detail: Importance of Anxiety and Depression Screening in HF

source_row.stem: A nurse supports a client's psychological adjustment to living with chronic heart failure. This support includes:
source_row.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"Assuming the client needs fairly little ongoing psychosocial support once they become medically stable on their current heart failure treatment regimen","B":"Focusing mainly on medication adherence alone during clinic visits, with comparatively little attention paid to the client's broader emotional needs","C":"A single conversation held once at the time of diagnosis, with fairly little planned follow-up offered to the client in the months that follow","D":"Providing ongoing emotional support, connecting the client with resources, and addressing the unique challenges of managing a chronic, potentially progressive cardiac condition"}}
source_row.rationale: Supporting a client's psychological adjustment to chronic heart failure includes providing ongoing emotional support, connecting them with relevant resources (such as support groups), and addressing the unique challenges of managing a chronic, potentially progressive condition, recognizing that this adjustment process continues throughout the disease course.
source_row.source_name: AHA — Psychosocial Support in Chronic Heart Failure
source_row.source_detail: Comprehensive Support for Chronic HF Adjustment

source_row.stem: A nurse supports the family of a client with end-stage heart failure facing significant symptom burden and uncertain prognosis. This support includes:
source_row.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"Assuming every family requires essentially the same fixed approach to support, without individualizing that support based on their own specific circumstances","B":"Providing honest, compassionate communication, connecting the family with appropriate resources such as palliative care, and supporting their emotional and practical needs","C":"Focusing mainly on the client's own needs during visits, with comparatively little attention paid to the family members who are also affected","D":"Avoiding any discussion of prognosis with the family throughout the remainder of the client's hospital stay and beyond discharge"}}
source_row.rationale: Supporting the family of a client with end-stage heart failure includes providing honest, compassionate communication about the client's condition and prognosis, connecting the family with appropriate resources such as palliative care, and supporting their emotional and practical needs, individualized to each family's specific circumstances.
source_row.source_name: CAPC / AHA — Family Support in Advanced Heart Failure
source_row.source_detail: Comprehensive Family Support in End-Stage HF

source_row.stem: A nurse teaches a client with CKD to take a phosphate binder with meals. This medication works by:
source_row.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"Carrying fairly little effect on the client's serum phosphorus levels once the medication is actually taken","B":"Increasing how much phosphorus is absorbed from food within the intestine","C":"Directly filtering phosphorus out through the kidneys as its primary mechanism of action","D":"Binding dietary phosphorus in the GI tract, reducing its absorption into the bloodstream"}}
source_row.rationale: Phosphate binders work by binding dietary phosphorus in the GI tract, reducing its absorption into the bloodstream, an important strategy since impaired kidneys cannot adequately excrete excess phosphorus, and must be taken with meals to be effective.
source_row.source_name: FDA Prescribing Information — Phosphate Binders
source_row.source_detail: Mechanism of Action and Administration Timing

source_row.stem: A nurse administers cinacalcet, a calcimimetic, for a client with secondary hyperparathyroidism related to CKD. This medication works by:
source_row.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"Directly replacing the client's own vitamin D stores as its primary mechanism of action","B":"Increasing the sensitivity of calcium-sensing receptors on the parathyroid gland, reducing PTH secretion","C":"Carrying fairly little effect on the client's parathyroid hormone levels once treatment has actually begun","D":"Increasing parathyroid hormone secretion as its primary intended pharmacologic effect"}}
source_row.rationale: Calcimimetics like cinacalcet work by increasing the sensitivity of calcium-sensing receptors on the parathyroid gland, reducing parathyroid hormone secretion, used to manage secondary hyperparathyroidism common in CKD.
source_row.source_name: FDA Prescribing Information — Cinacalcet
source_row.source_detail: Mechanism of Action as a Calcimimetic

source_row.stem: A nurse administers a vitamin D analog, such as calcitriol, for a client with CKD-related mineral bone disease. This medication is used because:
source_row.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"Vitamin D carrying fairly little relevance to the renal bone disease that develops as a complication of chronic kidney disease","B":"This medication being used mainly to treat an unrelated condition rather than the client's CKD-related mineral bone disease","C":"Impaired kidneys tending to produce an excess of active vitamin D rather than too little of it","D":"Impaired kidneys have reduced ability to activate vitamin D, so an active analog helps support calcium absorption and PTH regulation"}}
source_row.rationale: Impaired kidneys have reduced ability to convert vitamin D to its active form, so an active vitamin D analog like calcitriol helps support calcium absorption and appropriate PTH regulation, addressing CKD-related mineral and bone disease.
source_row.source_name: FDA Prescribing Information — Calcitriol
source_row.source_detail: Rationale for Active Vitamin D Analog Use in CKD

source_row.stem: A nurse administers IV iron sucrose for a client with CKD-related anemia and iron deficiency. IV iron is often preferred over oral iron in this population because:
source_row.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"Oral iron generally being absorbed and utilized more quickly and far more reliably by the body than IV iron in clients who have chronic kidney disease","B":"Absorption of oral iron can be limited in CKD, and IV administration ensures more reliable iron delivery, particularly important for clients also receiving erythropoiesis-stimulating agents","C":"IV iron carrying fairly little established role in managing anemia related to chronic kidney disease in most clients receiving ongoing hemodialysis treatment sessions","D":"Oral iron generally having fairly few absorption limitations in clients who have chronic kidney disease compared with the general adult population"}}
source_row.rationale: IV iron is often preferred over oral iron in CKD because oral iron absorption can be limited in this population, and IV administration ensures more reliable iron delivery, particularly important for clients also receiving erythropoiesis-stimulating agents who need adequate iron stores for effective response.
source_row.source_name: FDA Prescribing Information — Iron Sucrose
source_row.source_detail: Rationale for IV Iron Preference in CKD

source_row.stem: A nurse understands that ARBs, like ACE inhibitors, are used in clients with CKD and proteinuria because they:
source_row.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"Directly curing the client's underlying kidney disease once the medication has actually been started","B":"Can help reduce proteinuria and slow progression of kidney disease through effects on glomerular pressure","C":"Carrying fairly little effect on renal outcomes despite their known role in reducing proteinuria","D":"Being considered contraindicated in essentially every client who has some degree of kidney disease"}}
source_row.rationale: ARBs, similar to ACE inhibitors, can help reduce proteinuria and slow progression of kidney disease through their effects on glomerular pressure, an important renal-protective strategy in appropriate clients with CKD and proteinuria.
source_row.source_name: KDIGO — CKD Management Guidelines
source_row.source_detail: Renal Protective Effects of ARBs

source_row.stem: A nurse administers patiromer for a client with CKD and chronic hyperkalemia. This medication works by:
source_row.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"Binding potassium in the GI tract, increasing its fecal excretion and lowering serum potassium over time","B":"Providing immediate, emergency-level potassium reduction suitable for a client in acute hyperkalemic crisis","C":"Carrying fairly little effect on the client's serum potassium level once the medication is actually taken","D":"Increasing how much potassium is absorbed from food within the gastrointestinal tract"}}
source_row.rationale: Patiromer works by binding potassium in the GI tract, increasing its fecal excretion and lowering serum potassium over time, used for chronic management of hyperkalemia rather than as an emergency treatment given its slower onset of action.
source_row.source_name: FDA Prescribing Information — Patiromer
source_row.source_detail: Mechanism and Onset of Action

source_row.stem: A nurse administers sodium polystyrene sulfonate for a client with hyperkalemia. The nurse should be aware this medication:
source_row.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"Having an extremely rapid onset of action that makes it well suited for treating emergent, severe episodes of hyperkalemia","B":"Has a relatively slower onset of action and is generally not relied upon as the sole treatment for severe, emergent hyperkalemia","C":"Carrying fairly little effect on the client's serum potassium level once the medication has actually been taken","D":"Being administered to the client only through the intravenous route rather than by mouth or as an enema"}}
source_row.rationale: Sodium polystyrene sulfonate has a relatively slower onset of action, so it is generally not relied upon as the sole treatment for severe, emergent hyperkalemia, which requires more rapid-acting interventions (such as calcium, insulin/glucose, or dialysis) alongside or instead of this agent.
source_row.source_name: FDA Prescribing Information — Sodium Polystyrene Sulfonate
source_row.source_detail: Onset of Action and Role in Emergent Hyperkalemia

source_row.stem: A nurse teaches a client that sevelamer, a non-calcium phosphate binder, may be preferred over calcium-based binders in certain clients because it:
source_row.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"Avoids adding to the client's overall calcium load, which may be preferred in clients at risk for vascular calcification or with elevated calcium levels","B":"Providing the client with additional calcium supplementation beyond what a calcium-based phosphate binder would already typically offer","C":"Being administered to the client through an injection rather than taken by mouth alongside each of their meals","D":"Carrying fairly little phosphate-binding activity at all, despite being classified specifically as a non-calcium phosphate binder"}}
source_row.rationale: Sevelamer, a non-calcium phosphate binder, may be preferred over calcium-based binders in certain clients because it avoids adding to the overall calcium load, which may be beneficial in clients at risk for vascular calcification or those with already elevated calcium levels.
source_row.source_name: FDA Prescribing Information — Sevelamer
source_row.source_detail: Non-Calcium Binder Rationale

source_row.stem: A nurse teaches a client taking calcium acetate as a phosphate binder to monitor for signs of:
source_row.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"Only phosphorus-related effects, with fairly little attention needed toward the client's calcium levels","B":"Hypercalcemia, since calcium-based phosphate binders add to the client's overall calcium intake","C":"Hypocalcemia specifically, the opposite of what a calcium-based phosphate binder would actually be expected to cause","D":"Fairly few calcium-related effects worth monitoring for in a client taking this particular phosphate binder"}}
source_row.rationale: Calcium acetate, a calcium-based phosphate binder, adds to the client's overall calcium intake, so clients should be monitored for signs of hypercalcemia, an important consideration when selecting and monitoring phosphate binder therapy.
source_row.source_name: FDA Prescribing Information — Calcium Acetate
source_row.source_detail: Hypercalcemia Risk with Calcium-Based Binders

source_row.stem: A nurse administers epoetin alfa for a client with CKD-related anemia. The nurse should ensure adequate iron stores before and during treatment because:
source_row.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"Adequate iron is necessary to support the increased red blood cell production stimulated by epoetin, and iron deficiency can limit treatment response","B":"Iron monitoring being considered relevant mainly for clients receiving oral iron therapy, rather than for clients on epoetin alfa","C":"Epoetin alfa itself providing the client with its own built-in iron supplementation throughout the course of treatment","D":"Iron carrying fairly little established relationship to how effectively this particular medication actually ends up working"}}
source_row.rationale: Adequate iron stores are necessary to support the increased red blood cell production stimulated by erythropoiesis-stimulating agents like epoetin alfa, and iron deficiency can limit treatment response, requiring iron status monitoring and supplementation as needed.
source_row.source_name: FDA Prescribing Information — Epoetin Alfa
source_row.source_detail: Importance of Adequate Iron Stores with ESA Therapy

source_row.stem: A nurse implements infection prevention measures for a client's dialysis access site. General principles include:
source_row.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"Strict aseptic technique during access cannulation or catheter care, and client education on monitoring for signs of infection","B":"Fairly few precautions actually needed beyond what standard hospital care would already typically provide","C":"Allowing essentially any staff member to access the site without any specific technique requirements in place","D":"Precautions considered relevant mainly for catheter access, rather than for fistulas or grafts as well"}}
source_row.rationale: Dialysis access infection prevention includes strict aseptic technique during access cannulation (for fistulas/grafts) or catheter care, along with client education on monitoring for signs of infection, applicable across all access types given the significant infection risk associated with repeated vascular access.
source_row.source_name: CDC — Dialysis Infection Prevention Guidelines
source_row.source_detail: General Access Infection Prevention Principles

source_row.stem: A nurse teaches a client with a new AV fistula about site care. Key teaching points include:
source_row.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"Fairly few specific precautions actually being needed once a fistula is considered healthy and fully well established","B":"Avoiding blood pressure measurements, venipuncture, and IV access on the fistula arm, and monitoring for signs of infection or malfunction","C":"Restricting all movement of the fistula arm permanently, regardless of how well the fistula is actually functioning over time","D":"Allowing blood pressure measurements and IV access to be performed on the fistula arm just as they would on any other arm"}}
source_row.rationale: AV fistula care teaching includes avoiding blood pressure measurements, venipuncture, and IV access on the fistula arm (to protect this vital access), and monitoring for signs of infection or malfunction (such as loss of thrill or bruit), essential for maintaining long-term access viability.
source_row.source_name: Fistula First / CDC — AV Fistula Care Guidelines
source_row.source_detail: Key AV Fistula Protection Teaching Points

source_row.stem: A nurse provides care for a client's dialysis catheter, using strict sterile technique. This heightened precaution level is important because:
source_row.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"Sterile technique being needed mainly for the initial catheter insertion procedure itself, rather than for its ongoing daily maintenance and care afterward","B":"Dialysis catheters carrying fairly little more infection risk overall than any other standard peripheral IV line that might otherwise be placed","C":"Central venous dialysis catheters provide direct access to central circulation and carry a significant risk of serious bloodstream infection if not managed with strict sterile technique","D":"Catheter-related infections generally carrying fairly little serious clinical consequence for the client who happens to develop one during treatment"}}
source_row.rationale: Central venous dialysis catheters provide direct access to central circulation and carry a significant risk of serious bloodstream infection if not managed with strict sterile technique for both insertion and all ongoing care, given the repeated access needed for dialysis treatments.
source_row.source_name: CDC — Dialysis Catheter Care Guidelines
source_row.source_detail: Rationale for Strict Sterile Catheter Care

source_row.stem: A nurse teaches a client performing home peritoneal dialysis about exit site care. This includes:
source_row.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"Fairly little specific site care actually being needed once the peritoneal dialysis catheter has first been placed","B":"Care considered relevant mainly during the initial healing period, with fairly little ongoing monitoring needed afterward","C":"Daily site cleansing per protocol, monitoring for signs of infection, and keeping the site dry unless specifically directed otherwise","D":"Submerging the exit site in bath water on a fairly regular basis as part of routine daily hygiene"}}
source_row.rationale: Peritoneal dialysis exit site care includes daily site cleansing per established protocol, ongoing monitoring for signs of infection (redness, drainage, pain), and generally keeping the site dry, an important ongoing self-care skill for clients on home peritoneal dialysis.
source_row.source_name: ISPD — Peritoneal Dialysis Exit Site Care Guidelines
source_row.source_detail: Key Exit Site Care Teaching Points

source_row.stem: A dialysis facility maintains strict water treatment and quality monitoring protocols. This is important because:
source_row.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"Water treatment protocols being considered relevant mainly to peritoneal dialysis specifically, rather than to hemodialysis treatment as well at the same facility","B":"Water quality monitoring being treated as an entirely optional step that is left up to each individual dialysis facility's own internal preference","C":"Water quality carrying fairly little established relevance to the overall safety of the entire hemodialysis treatment process performed at the facility","D":"Water used in the dialysis process comes into contact with the client's blood (via the dialysate), so contamination could introduce pathogens or toxins directly into the bloodstream"}}
source_row.rationale: Strict water treatment and quality monitoring is critical in dialysis facilities because water used in the dialysis process comes into contact with the client's blood (via the dialysate across the dialyzer membrane), so contamination could introduce pathogens or toxins directly into the bloodstream, a unique and serious safety consideration in hemodialysis.
source_row.source_name: CDC — Dialysis Water Treatment Safety Guidelines
source_row.source_detail: Importance of Water Quality in Hemodialysis Safety

source_row.stem: A dialysis nurse follows specific safety protocols when cannulating an AV fistula with large-bore needles. These protocols are important because:
source_row.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"Standard precautions generally being considered inapplicable to the specific context of dialysis needle use","B":"Large-bore dialysis needles carry increased needlestick injury risk, requiring careful technique and appropriate safety-engineered devices","C":"Safety precautions being considered relevant mainly for catheter-based access, rather than for fistula cannulation as well","D":"Fistula cannulation carrying fairly few unique safety considerations compared with other vascular access procedures"}}
source_row.rationale: Large-bore dialysis needles used for AV fistula/graft cannulation carry increased needlestick injury risk given their size, requiring careful technique and use of appropriate safety-engineered devices to protect staff, consistent with standard bloodborne pathogen precautions.
source_row.source_name: OSHA — Needlestick Safety in Dialysis Settings
source_row.source_detail: Needlestick Risk with Large-Bore Dialysis Needles

source_row.stem: A dialysis unit implements specific infection control measures given the population's increased risk for bloodborne pathogen transmission. These measures may include:
source_row.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"Dedicated equipment for known infected clients in some cases, along with strict adherence to standard precautions and equipment disinfection protocols between clients","B":"Fairly few specific infection control measures actually being implemented beyond what standard hospital-wide precautions would already typically cover","C":"Declining to provide dialysis care altogether to any client who happens to have a known bloodborne infection diagnosed","D":"Measures considered relevant mainly during active outbreak situations specifically, rather than as part of routine, everyday dialysis unit operations"}}
source_row.rationale: Dialysis units implement specific infection control measures given the population's recognized increased risk for bloodborne pathogen transmission, which may include dedicated equipment for known infected clients in some circumstances, along with strict standard precautions and thorough equipment disinfection between all clients.
source_row.source_name: CDC — Dialysis Bloodborne Pathogen Prevention Guidelines
source_row.source_detail: Enhanced Precautions in Dialysis Settings

source_row.stem: A dialysis nurse performs hand hygiene at multiple points during a single client's treatment session, including before and after any contact with the access site or equipment. This frequent hand hygiene is important because:
source_row.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"A single hand hygiene episode performed once per client visit generally being considered sufficient for the entire session","B":"Hand hygiene carrying fairly little established role in preventing infection within the dialysis setting specifically","C":"The dialysis process involves multiple points of potential contamination given the frequent, direct vascular access required","D":"Hand hygiene being considered somewhat less important in dialysis settings compared with other clinical care areas"}}
source_row.rationale: Frequent hand hygiene throughout a dialysis session is important because the dialysis process involves multiple points of potential contamination given the frequent, direct vascular access required, making consistent hand hygiene at each transition point a critical infection prevention practice.
source_row.source_name: CDC — Hand Hygiene in Dialysis Settings
source_row.source_detail: Importance of Frequent Hand Hygiene During Dialysis

source_row.stem: A nephrology nurse's role typically involves:
source_row.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"Providing care for clients across the spectrum of kidney disease, including CKD management, dialysis care, and transplant support","B":"A role limited mainly to hemodialysis unit settings, rather than spanning the broader continuum of kidney disease care","C":"Fairly little involvement in providing patient education as part of the nephrology nurse's overall role","D":"Mostly administrative scheduling tasks, with fairly little direct clinical involvement in the nurse's day-to-day work"}}
source_row.rationale: A nephrology nurse's role typically involves providing care for clients across the spectrum of kidney disease, including CKD management, dialysis care (hemodialysis and peritoneal dialysis), and transplant support, spanning multiple care settings.
source_row.source_name: American Nephrology Nurses Association — Scope of Practice
source_row.source_detail: Scope of Nephrology Nursing Role

source_row.stem: A dialysis technician works alongside nursing staff in a dialysis unit. Their scope of practice typically includes:
source_row.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"Fairly little role in direct client care of any kind as part of the dialysis technician's overall scope of practice","B":"Independent, unsupervised clinical decision-making considered essentially equivalent to that of a registered nurse","C":"Specific technical tasks, such as machine setup and monitoring during dialysis, performed under appropriate supervision per state regulations","D":"A scope of practice considered essentially identical across every state, with fairly little regional variation involved"}}
source_row.rationale: Dialysis technicians typically perform specific technical tasks, such as machine setup and monitoring during dialysis treatment, under appropriate supervision, with the specific scope of practice varying by state regulations regarding technician roles in dialysis care.
source_row.source_name: CMS — Dialysis Facility Staffing Requirements
source_row.source_detail: Scope of Dialysis Technician Practice

source_row.stem: A nurse learns about the role of ESRD Networks in the United States. These organizations are involved in:
source_row.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"Fairly little established function within the broader U.S. healthcare system as it specifically relates to kidney disease care","B":"Mainly research-related activities, with fairly little direct clinical relevance to patients actually receiving dialysis treatment","C":"The direct, hands-on provision of dialysis treatment itself, rather than oversight and coordination of that ongoing care","D":"Quality oversight, data collection, and patient advocacy related to end-stage renal disease care within their designated geographic regions"}}
source_row.rationale: ESRD Networks are involved in quality oversight, data collection, and patient advocacy related to end-stage renal disease care within their designated geographic regions, functioning under CMS contract to support quality improvement in dialysis care nationally.
source_row.source_name: CMS — ESRD Network Program Overview
source_row.source_detail: Function and Purpose of ESRD Networks

source_row.stem: A dialysis facility must comply with specific federal regulations, known as Conditions for Coverage, to participate in Medicare. These regulations address:
source_row.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"Only financial billing practices at the facility, with fairly little attention paid to actual clinical care standards","B":"Comprehensive standards including patient care, infection control, water quality, and quality assessment/performance improvement","C":"Requirements considered essentially identical to those that apply to any general outpatient clinic elsewhere","D":"Fairly few specific clinical care requirements actually built into these particular federal regulations"}}
source_row.rationale: CMS Conditions for Coverage for dialysis facilities address comprehensive standards including patient care, infection control, water quality, and quality assessment/performance improvement, reflecting the unique and significant safety considerations specific to dialysis care delivery.
source_row.source_name: CMS — ESRD Conditions for Coverage
source_row.source_detail: Scope of Dialysis Facility Regulatory Requirements
